top_strength: Zachary is clean and unhesitating on rate mechanics, and he answers a pricing question the first time it's asked without hedging. When the customer probed whether a short move gets billed down, Zachary gave the exact right answer in one breath: 'Fifteen minute, increments and yes, let's say it only takes four hours that's all you would pay for just the time actually worked.' Same on materials — the customer went item by item (blankets, shrink wrap, TVs) and got a straight yes each time, capped by a genuinely good micro-explanation of TV handling: 'we just handle that like a, not a normal piece of furniture. We'll unmount it if we need to remove any fee or base wrap it in our premium moving blankets and then lightly stretcher up on top of that.' That specificity is what turned a price shopper into a booking in under six minutes. He also gets credit for pace — this was an efficient, no-wasted-motion call that ended in a scheduled job.
coaching_note: Zachary priced the job before he knew anything about it, and never went back to fix it. The customer said 'two bedroom apartment' and Zachary's very next substantive line was 'So we charge $101 per hour per mover for this move... on average it typically takes a two man crew around six hours.' Only after the customer had already committed did he learn it's a 4th-floor apartment ('It's on the fourth floor, we have elevators') with 25 boxes going to a single-family home whose stairs he never asked about — and the six-hour number never moved. That is the estimate-accuracy problem in miniature: the estimate wasn't wrong because the rep guessed badly, it was wrong because it was issued before intake. The fix is sequencing, not skill — gather floor, elevator, walk, boxes, and destination stairs first, then quote a range and name the variables that push it up. The second cost here is that the customer bought purely on price, because nothing else was ever offered: no No Worries coverage, no Meet Your Mover, no On-Time Guarantee, no no-deposit, and no prep speech at all. A 4th-floor apartment with 25 boxes is the single best Save Your Ass candidate on the board — a carload of loose items and consolidated drawers is real money off this bill — and it went unsaid.
phone_presence_notes: Polite, responsive and easy to follow, but purely transactional — no affirmations, no empathy markers, the customer's name is never used once, and every question on the call came from the customer, though the close stayed positive ('No problem at all. We'll see you on the twenty seventh.').
